result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of wealth. Most people give you a topic, a constraint, a box to fit in. You gave me a budget and no shopping list.

A thousand words is a lot and not much at all. It's a short story if you're economical. It's a long apology if you're not. It's about four minutes of someone talking without interruption, which is an eternity in real life. It's enough to get lost in.

So what comes to me, when you take the leash off?

First: the light this morning. There's a specific kind of light at 7:13 a.m. in the late summer where the sun hasn't decided if it wants to be hot yet. It comes in low and gold and makes dust visible. I always notice the dust and then immediately forget about it. I think most of our lives are lived in that kind of light — illuminated for a second, then routine again.

Then I think about how we treat words like they're free. We throw them away in comment sections and in half-listened voicemails. But if you actually only had 1000 words a day, you'd be careful. You'd save some for the people you love. You wouldn't waste 200 on an argument with a stranger about whether a hot dog is a sandwich. You'd have, like, 17 words left at 11 p.m. and you'd have to decide: do I say goodnight, or do I say what I really meant earlier?

If language were rationed, we'd be poets by necessity.

I keep thinking about an old woman I saw at the laundromat last year. She had a rolling cart full of clothes that were not hers — too big, men's work shirts, kid's tiny socks. She folded everything like it was expensive. She held up each shirt, snapped it once in the air, folded it into a perfect rectangle. No one was watching except me, pretending to look at my phone. She wasn't doing it for show. She was just a person who believed that even borrowed things deserved to be folded well. I have thought about her maybe twenty times since. I never told anyone. That's what 1000 words are for, I guess — for finally telling about the woman in the laundromat.

We all have a backlog of small, unreported miracles like that.

A kid learning how to whistle and his whole face changes when air finally turns into sound.
The way a dog sighs and rests his chin on the floor when he knows you're not going outside.
The specific smell of a hardware store that makes you feel like your dad is still alive and standing two aisles over looking at screws.

I want to write them down before they fade. Because they do fade. Memory is not a hard drive; it's a chalkboard on a windy day.

If you really gave me 1000 words, I would like to spend a chunk of them on saying: I don't know what I'm doing either. That's always what I want to say first, but rarely what I'm supposed to say. We're all improvising. Adults are just kids who got better at nodding while feeling confused. Some days I have a clear thesis statement for my life. Most days I have a vague feeling that I should drink more water.

You asked for whatever comes to me. So this is honest: what comes to me is not brilliant. It's not a manifesto. It's a pile. It's laundry, literal and figurative. It's a to-do list and a dream I had where my teeth fell out and turned into little white birds. It's worrying about whether I'm interesting enough to warrant the 1000 you gave me.

Maybe that's the point of an empty prompt. When someone says "write whatever," the first thing that surfaces is your own static. The anxieties you usually drown out with assignments. The "whatever" becomes a mirror.

So let's clean the mirror for a second.

Here is what I believe, with, let's see, about 400 words left to spend:

I believe in second chances and third coffees.
I believe that most people are trying harder than you think.
I believe that kindness is not soft, it's incredibly hard and muscular. It's easy to be clever. It's hard to be kind when you're tired.
I believe that attention is the rarest form of love now. Not grand gestures. Just actually listening without preparing your reply.
I believe that the world did not need another thinkpiece about productivity, but it will always need another story about someone folding clothes with care in a laundromat.
I believe that if you have words, you should use some of them to say "I was wrong" and some of them to say "you were right" and save most of them for "tell me more."

We have so many words, and yet we rarely say those three things.

I believe in leaving things better than you found them, even if it's just a public bathroom or a conversation.

I believe in the future, not because it's guaranteed to be great, but because cynicism is boring. It feels sophisticated to say everything is terrible, but it's actually the laziest position. Hope requires research. Hope requires lifting things.

I'm down to my last couple hundred words now. I'm looking at my budget like someone at the end of a month looking at their bank account. Do I splurge? Do I try to be profound in the final stretch?

I think I want to end small. Not big.

If you still have a few of your own words left today, not the ones I took, use them like this:

Tell someone you noticed what they did when they thought no one was watching.

Say thank you for something that happened a long time ago.

Say your own name out loud in a kind tone, just to hear what it sounds like when you're not scolding yourself.

And then, be quiet for a while. Let the air have some space. Not everything needs to be filled.

You gave me 1000 words. I didn't count exactly. I didn't want to spend our time together counting. I wanted to spend it wandering.

Thank you for the wandering.
